title: A river that cuts through a mountain
teaches: How rivers cut down to base level, and how a river can come to cross a mountain range rather than go around it

blocks.text: In May 1869 John Wesley Powell, a one-armed Civil War veteran and professor of geology, set off down the Green River in Wyoming Territory with nine men and four wooden boats to explore the canyons of the Green and the Colorado, the last large blank on the map of the United States. Two weeks in, after floating through an open valley called Browns Park, the river turned straight into the Uinta Mountains. Its course there was a narrow canyon walled by red sandstone cliffs some 700 metres high. A member of the crew suggested naming it the Canyon of Lodore, after a poem by Robert Southey about a roaring cataract. In its rapids they wrecked a boat and lost a third of their rations.

blocks.caption: Where the Green River leaves Browns Park and enters the eastern Uinta Mountains through the Canyon of Lodore.

options.title: The Canyon of Lodore
options.alt: A shaded relief map of the eastern end of the Uinta Mountains: the open valley of Browns Park in the north, and the Green River's canyon cutting south through the mountains to Echo Park.

blocks.text: The puzzle struck Powell at once. The Uintas are a range of mountains, and a river in open country could easily have gone around their eastern end, where the land is lower. Instead it heads directly into the range and cuts right through it. Water does not run uphill, so either the river was there before the mountains rose, or the mountains had once been buried and hidden from view, or something else had happened. Powell spent the next several years thinking about how rivers shape the land, and his answers, together with those of his younger colleague Grove Karl Gilbert, laid the foundations for the study of landforms.

blocks.caption: The Gates of Lodore, where the Green River enters the Uinta Mountains.

blocks.title: Hold on to
points: The Green River leaves the open valley of Browns Park and cuts straight through the Uinta Mountains in the Canyon of Lodore, even though lower ground lies around the end of the range.

blocks.text: Powell's first principle was simple: a river can cut down only as far as the body of water it flows into. "We may consider the level of the sea to be a grand base level, below which the dry lands cannot be eroded," he wrote in 1875. A lake or a larger river acts as a local base level for the streams that drain into it. Every river works its bed down toward its base level, and over time its long profile, the curve of its bed from source to mouth, settles into a smooth arc, steep near the headwaters and nearly flat at the mouth, just steep enough at every point to carry the water and sediment supplied to it. Gilbert called a river in this state **graded**.

When base level drops, whether because sea level falls or because the land rises, the river is no longer graded. It begins to cut down at its mouth, and the steepened reach where the old and new profiles meet, a step known as a **knickpoint**, retreats upstream as the river erodes backward into its bed. Often a knickpoint shows up as a waterfall or a run of rapids. Niagara Falls is one: since the ice sheets retreated, the falls have worked about 11 kilometres back from the edge of the Niagara Escarpment, a long cliff of limestone and dolostone, at roughly a metre a year before engineers diverted much of the river's water for hydroelectric power. Gilbert used that rate of retreat to estimate how long ago the ice had left.

blocks.caption: A river's long profile, from source (left) to mouth (right). The dashed line shows the river before its base level fell.
blocks.task: Drop the base level and let the knickpoint climb at least 40% of the way upstream

blocks.text: Because a knickpoint takes time to travel, a fall in base level works its way through a drainage basin slowly. The lower reaches of a river are cut down first, while the headwaters may remain untouched for tens or hundreds of thousands of years. Old river terraces stranded high on valley walls and waterfalls far upstream are often the mark of a knickpoint still making its way inland.

blocks.caption: Palouse Falls in eastern Washington, where the Palouse River drops over a step in its bed about 60 metres high.

blocks.title: Hold on to
points: Base level, usually the sea or a lake, is the lowest elevation to which a river can erode its bed.
A graded river has worked its bed into a smooth concave profile, steep near its source and gentle near its mouth, adjusted to carry its load of water and sediment.
When base level falls, a steep step called a knickpoint (often a waterfall or rapids) migrates upstream, slowing as the drainage area shrinks.

blocks.text: To account for the Canyon of Lodore, Powell proposed that the Green River had been flowing along its present course before the Uintas existed. As the range rose slowly across its path, the river cut down as fast as the rock was lifted, holding its course while the mountains grew around it. "The river preserved its level," he wrote, "but the mountains were lifted up; as the saw revolves on a fixed pivot, while the log through which it cuts is moved along." In this image the river is the saw, held at a fixed elevation, and the rising range is the log pushed up into the blade. Powell called such a river **antecedent**, meaning that it predates the geological structure it crosses.

Whether a river can pull this off depends on a race between uplift and erosion. A ridge rising across a river's path goes up at some rate; the river can cut down at another rate, governed by how much water it carries, how steep its bed is, and how stubborn the rock is. If the river cuts at least as fast as the ridge rises, it keeps its course and saws a narrowing canyon through the crest. If uplift outpaces erosion, the riverbed in the gap is lifted, water ponds into a lake upstream, and eventually the lake spills out around the end of the ridge, abandoning the old gorge and leaving a high, dry notch in the skyline known as a **wind gap**.

blocks.caption: A ridge rising across a river's path, seen along the river. Brown is the ridge; blue is the river and any lake ponded behind the ridge.
blocks.task: Find rates at which the river keeps its course and cuts a canyon at least 700 m deep

blocks.text: True antecedent rivers do exist. In Washington State, the Yakima River winds in deep, tight meanders through Yakima Canyon, slicing across basalt ridges that folded upward after the meandering river was already established. Along the border of Washington and Oregon, the Columbia River crosses the entire Cascade Range through the Columbia River Gorge, holding on to a path it followed as the range rose across it. Several great rivers of the Himalaya, including the Indus, the Sutlej, and the Brahmaputra, rise north of the highest peaks and cut south through some of the deepest gorges on Earth, having kept their courses as the mountains were pushed up.

blocks.caption: The Yakima River seen from Umtanum Ridge, one of the basalt ridges it cuts through.

blocks.title: Hold on to
points: An antecedent river is older than the ridge or range it crosses, having maintained its course by cutting down as fast as the rock rose.
If uplift outpaces incision, the river is dammed and diverted around the obstacle, leaving its former canyon high and dry as a wind gap.
The Yakima River in Yakima Canyon and the Columbia River in the Columbia River Gorge are classic antecedent courses.

blocks.text: For the Green River itself, Powell's explanation turned out to be wrong. The Uinta Mountains were pushed up during the Laramide mountain-building episode between about 70 and 40 million years ago, whereas the Green River's course through them is no more than a few million years old, almost certainly less than 8 million. The river arrived long after the mountains stood there.

Powell himself had outlined a second way a river can come to cross a range. If an old mountain belt is worn down and buried beneath a blanket of younger sediment, a river can establish a course across the smooth plain above with no trace of the buried ridges below. As the river later cuts down, it encounters the hard rock of the buried range and is locked into its slot, sawing a canyon into the ancient structure while erosion strips away the softer cover on either side. A river let down onto older structures in this way is called **superimposed**. At Lodore, the eastern Uintas had been partly buried by the sediments that still floor Browns Park, and the eastern end of the range had also dropped along faults. Most geologists now think the Green River found its way across that lowered, sediment-draped end of the range, through a combination of burial and a lake spilling over a low divide, and then entrenched itself in the hard sandstone as regional uplift and the integration of the Colorado River system lowered its base level.

The exact balance between burial and spillover at Lodore is still debated, yet every modern reconstruction rests on the principles Powell and Gilbert worked out: rivers cut toward a base level, the competition between incision and uplift decides whether a channel holds its course, and a canyon sliced straight through a mountain range is proof that the landscape around the river has changed profoundly since the river began to flow.

blocks.title: Hold on to
points: The Green River at Lodore is tens of millions of years younger than the Uinta Mountains, so its canyon cannot be purely antecedent.
A superimposed river establishes its course on a younger cover of sediment or rock and keeps that course as it cuts down into older, buried structures beneath.

blocks.caption: Five questions on rivers and base level
blocks.task: Select the best answer for each question

items.ask: What determines a river's ultimate base level, and why can the river not cut deeper?
choices: The elevation of the sea or lake it drains into, because water loses its slope and flow velocity once it reaches standing water
The elevation of the river's headwaters, which sets the total potential energy of the stream
The depth of the water in the channel during the largest annual flood
items.why: A river relies on a downhill slope to flow and erode its bed; once it reaches the level of the sea or lake it empties into, it can no longer cut downward.

items.ask: If sea level drops by 50 metres, how do the headwaters of a long river respond in the first few centuries?
choices: They show no change yet, because the steepened knickpoint must erode all the way upstream from the mouth before they feel the drop
They immediately incise 50 metres to match the new sea level
They aggrade their beds with sediment to compensate for the steeper mouth
items.why: A drop in base level is felt first at the mouth. The resulting knickpoint migrates upstream over thousands of years, slowing down as the river narrows toward its source.

items.ask: Under Powell's model of an antecedent river, how does a river come to cut straight through a mountain range?
choices: The river was already flowing along that path before the mountains existed, and it cut downward as fast as the range rose across it
The river followed an open fault canyon that had split the range apart before the water arrived
Extreme glacial floods briefly pushed the river over the crest of the range
items.why: In Powell's saw-and-log analogy, the river holds its level like a fixed saw blade while tectonic uplift pushes the mountain range upward into it.

items.ask: A tectonic ridge rises at 1 mm per year across a river whose maximum incision rate in that rock is 0.3 mm per year. What is the long-term outcome?
choices: The riverbed in the gap is lifted, a lake ponds upstream, and the river is eventually deflected around the ridge, leaving a dry wind gap
The river saws a narrow canyon 1 kilometre deep after one million years
The weight of the river water suppresses uplift along that section of the ridge
items.why: Because uplift outpaces incision, the ridge wins the race. The defeated river is ponded and diverted, and its abandoned notch is left high on the ridge as a wind gap.

items.ask: What piece of geological evidence ruled out Powell's idea that the Green River at Lodore is simply antecedent to the Uinta Mountains?
choices: The Uintas were uplifted 70 to 40 million years ago, whereas the Green River established its course through them less than about 8 million years ago
The red sandstones in the Canyon of Lodore are softer than the sediments in Browns Park
The Green River flows south through the range whereas tectonic compression came from the north
items.why: An antecedent river must be older than the structure it crosses. Because the Uintas rose tens of millions of years before the Green River arrived, the river had to cross the already-formed range across a buried or fault-lowered surface.

learned: Rivers erode downward toward a base level and adjust their beds into a smooth, graded profile that is steep near the source and gentle near the mouth.
A drop in base level creates a steepened reach called a knickpoint, often a waterfall or rapids, which erodes progressively upstream.
A river that cuts through a mountain range may be antecedent (older than the uplift) or superimposed (let down onto an older range from a younger cover of sediment).
The Green River at Lodore is millions of years younger than the Uinta Mountains it crosses, having established its path over a partly buried and fault-lowered end of the range.
